subtitle: One stray n/a or $ sign, and a whole numeric column turns into text.

eyebrow: The practice data — everything arrived as text
caption: object is pandas' catch-all for text — run dtypes or info() first on any new dataset.

eyebrow: Text to numbers — the direct approach fails loudly
code:
df["amount"].astype(float)
# ValueError: could not convert string to float: '$1,200.50'

df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(
    df["amount"].str.replace(r"[$,]", "", regex=True), errors="coerce")
# 1200.50, 75.00, NaN, 310.25
caption: Strip the symbols first, then to_numeric with errors="coerce" turns n/a into an ordinary NaN.
NaT ("not a time") is the date equivalent of NaN — once real datetime64, you can filter by range or subtract.

code:
s = pd.Series(["03/05/2024"])
pd.to_datetime(s, format="%m/%d/%Y")   # 2024-03-05
pd.to_datetime(s, format="%d/%m/%Y")   # 2024-05-03
# both succeed -- only one is right!
caption: pandas won't warn you. Pass format= explicitly whenever you know the source's convention.

code:
df["order_id"] = df["order_id"].astype(int)
df["shipped"] = (df["shipped"].str.lower().str[0]
                 .map({"y": True, "n": False}))
df["tier"] = df["tier"].astype("category")
caption: Normalize text before mapping to booleans; astype(int) needs no NaN; category suits a fixed small set of labels.
